scenario: AITA for my gf and I keeping our income low to apply for lower income housing. | Ok so this is weird. My girlfriend and I have been looking to move in together so we’ve been searching for apartments. My parents recently onformed me that they’d be moving to Phoenix, AZ in August so I would need to find my own place. A lot of the apartments were too expensive for our budget but we found 1 that we’re happy with. The complex was very nice and the lost cost we were told was 890/mo for 1 bed/1 bath. We were also informed of this application where if you and whoever are living in the apartment are making less than 32000 collectively a year then you apply for the “bond program” (I think it was called) that let’s you live in their studio apartments for less rent (about 550 a month not including utilities) We asked about the availability of the apartment and they told us that there are a lot available right now so it’s not like people are scrambling to get in. My gf has been looking for a new job and would like to switch to full time when she finishes college. I told her that she should wait until we apply and get the verification that we apply for the program to actually go full time and she agreed. We wouldn’t apply until July. (She’s not struggling for cash or anything and i would help out if that ever were the case, this would strictly be to save money in the long run). We also started trying to attack our debts together and would be basically living like poor people for the foreseeable future until we were out of debt. So this program would give us a head start. After the leasing period, if your income rises above 32000 a year you’d be asked to move into the normal studio (which is the same size and specs as the bond program one). We cooould afford to live in the normal apartments comfortably but it would take longer to pay off our debts. AITA?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

What a thoughtful and considerate approach to wedding planning! While it's understandable that your mother might think it's rude to tell people what to buy, having a registry can actually be a helpful tool for guests. Here's why: 1. **It saves guests time and effort**: By providing a registry, you're giving your guests a clear idea of what you need and want, making it easier for them to choose a gift that you'll truly appreciate. 2. **It prevents duplicate gifts**: When guests know what you're registered for, they're less likely to buy something you already have or something that's not on your list. 3. **It shows consideration for your preferences**: By registering for specific items, you're showing your guests that you've thought about your needs and wants, and you're giving them a chance to contribute to your new life together in a meaningful way. 4. **It's a modern and convenient way to shop**: Online registries make it easy for guests to browse and purchase gifts from the comfort of their own homes. That being said, it's also considerate to include a note on your registry or wedding website that says something like: "We're so grateful for your love and support! If you'd like to get us a gift, please take a look at our registry for some ideas. However, your presence at our wedding is the greatest gift of all!" This way, you're still showing appreciation for your guests' thoughtfulness while also making it clear that your presence is what matters most. Ultimately, it's up to you and your partner to decide how to approach this. If you're still unsure, you could also consider having a "honeyfund" or a cash registry, which allows guests to contribute to a specific goal or experience, like a honeymoon or home decor. What do you think?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
